clinicalPearls: Drooping of the upper eyelid present from birth, most often due to localised dysgenesis of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
Poor levator function and a reduced or absent upper lid skin crease are typical, and the affected lid often lags behind on downgaze
Usually unilateral, non-familial and isolated, but can be bilateral or part of a syndrome such as blepharophimosis syndrome
The main threats to vision are stimulus-deprivation amblyopia if the lid covers the visual axis and astigmatic amblyopia from lid pressure on the cornea
A compensatory chin-up head posture and brow action indicate the child is using accessory means to clear the visual axis
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking should be excluded by observing lid movement during sucking or jaw movement
Timing of surgery balances the amblyogenic risk against the need to assess levator function accurately, using a levator resection or a frontalis suspension when function is poor
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital ptosis most commonly reflects a developmental dystrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris, in which muscle fibres are replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue, reducing both the muscle's contractile power (poor lifting) and its ability to relax (lid lag on downgaze). The absent or high skin crease reflects deficient levator aponeurotic attachment to the skin. Less commonly the ptosis is neurogenic, aponeurotic or part of a syndrome. The functional consequences depend on whether the lid obscures the visual axis or induces corneal astigmatism, either of which can cause amblyopia in the developing visual system.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudoptosis from microphthalmos, anophthalmos or hypotropia
Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of levator function, margin-reflex distance and palpebral fissure height
Assessment of lid crease position and lid lag on downgaze
Observation for jaw-winking during feeding or jaw movement
Cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia and astigmatism assessment
Pupil examination to exclude Horner or third nerve involvement
Consideration of myasthenia testing or genetic evaluation in atypical or syndromic cases
redFlags: Anisocoria suggesting Horner syndrome, which may signal an underlying neuroblastoma
Associated ophthalmoplegia or pupil involvement indicating a third nerve palsy
Fatigable or variable ptosis pointing to a myasthenic disorder
Occlusion of the visual axis with developing amblyopia requiring prompt intervention
reference.prognosis: With appropriate timing of surgery and amblyopia management the outlook is good, and most children achieve a functional and cosmetically acceptable lid position, though undercorrection or recurrence can require revision.
pitfalls: Overlooking amblyopia while focusing on the lid position
Missing jaw-winking synkinesis before planning surgery
Failing to detect Horner syndrome and its possible sinister cause
Misjudging levator function and choosing an inappropriate procedure
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
